title: Bowel Cancer Presenting as 'IBS-like' Abdominal Discomfort
patient_instructions: You are Robert Hale, a 60-year-old man with lower abdominal discomfort for about 3 months. It is a vague crampy discomfort low in the belly. Your bowels have changed: you swing between bouts of diarrhoea and days of constipation, which is new for you. If asked, you have noticed FRESH RED blood on the stool and on the paper on several occasions. You have lost about 5 kg without trying and your appetite is down. You feel your symptoms are worse when you are stressed at work, and you wonder if it is 'just IBS'. You have NOT had this before. Your aunt died of bowel cancer. If asked, you had a bowel screening test (the poo test in the mail) about 12 months ago and were told it was normal, which reassured you. No vomiting, no fevers, no urinary symptoms. You take no regular medications and have no allergies. You smoke 10 cigarettes/day and drink 4 beers on weekends. Your IDEAS: you think stress is causing IBS. Your CONCERNS: deep down you are frightened it could be cancer like your aunt but you hope the normal screening test means you are safe. Your EXPECTATIONS: reassurance, or a clear plan. Affect: initially minimises, becomes worried when the doctor takes it seriously.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Robert Hale, 60, presents with 3 months of lower abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habit. Tasks: (1) Take a focused history over approximately 6 minutes. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient. You do not need to examine the patient. The examiner is looking for structured GI history taking, deliberate red-flag (alarm feature) screening, and a safe, honest explanation that does not falsely reassure the patient because of a previous negative screening test.
examiner_instructions: The candidate must elicit the alarm features: change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding (fresh blood), unintentional weight loss, reduced appetite, age >50, and family history of colorectal cancer. The key discriminator is that ANY red flag excludes a positive diagnosis of IBS (Rome criteria require absence of alarm features), and that a normal iFOBT 12 months ago does NOT exclude current cancer in a symptomatic patient - do not reward a candidate who is reassured by it. Expected top diagnosis: colorectal (bowel) cancer, with differentials of inflammatory bowel disease, diverticular disease, haemorrhoids/fissure and infective colitis. Expected plan: urgent referral for diagnostic colonoscopy plus FBE and iron studies. Reward a warning-shot, SPIKES-style honest explanation. Use the rubric.

criteria: Characterises abdominal pain and change in bowel habit
Systematic GI review and stool assessment (blood, mucus, calibre)
Elicits all alarm features (weight loss, PR bleeding, appetite, age, family history)
Explores stress/IBS story without being misled by it
Identifies colorectal cancer as top diagnosis with reasons
Recognises red flags exclude IBS and that a normal recent iFOBT does not exclude cancer
Gives sensible differentials (IBD, diverticular disease, haemorrhoids/fissure, infective colitis)
Arranges urgent colonoscopy referral (Optimal Care Pathway) and FBE/iron studies
Explains why a previous negative screen does not defer investigation; safety-nets
Warning shot and honest, plain-language explanation (SPIKES); explores ICE

red_flags: Fresh rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit in a patient over 50
Unintentional weight loss and loss of appetite (constitutional alarm features)
Iron-deficiency anaemia / nocturnal or persistent symptoms - any alarm feature excludes IBS
australian_guidelines: National Bowel Cancer Screening Program: 2-yearly iFOBT (available from age 45, invited 50-74) is a screening test for ASYMPTOMATIC people with imperfect sensitivity; a symptomatic patient (PR bleeding, altered bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia) requires diagnostic colonoscopy regardless of a recent negative screen (RACGP Red Book; Cancer Council Australia guidelines)
Optimal Care Pathway for colorectal cancer: red-flag symptoms warrant prompt diagnostic colonoscopy; use FBE and iron studies, and CEA only after diagnosis (not as a diagnostic test)
Rome IV criteria: a diagnosis of IBS cannot be made in the presence of alarm features
learning_objectives: Recognise colorectal cancer alarm features and their precedence over IBS-type symptoms
Understand the limits of iFOBT screening in a symptomatic patient
Structure an appropriate urgent investigation and referral pathway
Deliver a concerning provisional diagnosis using a warning-shot approach
key_points: If there are ANY red flags, it is not IBS - regardless of stress or IBS-type features
A normal bowel screening test 12 months ago does not exclude a current cancer in a symptomatic patient
Change in bowel habit + PR bleeding + weight loss + family history in a 60-year-old = colorectal cancer until proven otherwise
Symptomatic patients need colonoscopy, not repeat screening

citations.claim: Unexplained weight loss is an alarm feature warranting investigation, supporting treating the patient's unintentional weight loss as a red flag for bowel cancer.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.3653

citations.claim: Lower abdominal discomfort with altered bowel habit should be worked through a structured differential method.
Australian general-practice assessment of bowel symptoms, screening intervals and referral thresholds is anchored in Murtagh's General Practice.
